descriptionChirho: To be pressed or constrained by an inner psychological or spiritual force, such as the compulsion of Christ's love (2 Cor 5:14), the distress of being torn between two desires (Phil 1:23), the urgency of the word's constraint upon Paul (Acts 18:5), or the anguish of awaiting a baptism of suffering (Lk 12:50). The multilingual glosses point to internal pressure and constriction: Arabic مُنْحَصِرٌ (hemmed in), German bedraengen (press hard), Hebrew מֵצִיק/נִלְחָץ (distressed/pressed), Spanish constreñido/angustiado, Korean 눌리노라/사로잡혔다 (oppressed/seized).

To press upon or crowd around physically, as a throng of people surrounding and jostling someone, or as an army hemming in a city with siege works. In Lk 8:45, the crowd presses upon Jesus (συνέχουσίν σε), and in Lk 19:43, enemies will press upon Jerusalem with embankments (συνέξουσίν σε). The glosses reflect physical compression: Arabic يُحيطونَ (surround), Hebrew לוֹחֲצִים/יֵצְרוּ (press/besiege), Korean 누르다/조이다 (press/squeeze), Spanish te aprietan/te apretarán.

To physically hold, seize, or shut up something, restraining by direct bodily contact. In Lk 22:63, the men holding Jesus in custody (συνέχοντες) are physically restraining him as a prisoner. In Acts 7:57, the crowd stops up their ears (συνέσχον τὰ ὦτα), physically closing them. The glosses emphasize physical control: Arabic مُمْسِكونَ/سَدُّوا (holding/blocking), Hebrew אוֹחֲזִים/אָטְמוּ (grasping/stopping up), Korean 잡고/막았다 (seizing/blocking), Spanish sosteniendo/taparon.

To be seized, gripped, or afflicted by disease, fever, fear, or some overwhelming condition, used in the passive/middle voice to describe persons suffering under the power of an ailment or overwhelming emotion. In Mt 4:24, the sick are those 'held' by various diseases (συνεχομένους); in Lk 4:38, Simon's mother-in-law is gripped by fever (συνεχομένη πυρετῷ); in Lk 8:37, the Gerasenes are seized with great fear (συνείχοντο φόβῳ); in Acts 28:8, Publius' father lies afflicted with fever (συνεχόμενον πυρετοῖς). The multilingual glosses consistently indicate passive suffering: Arabic مُصابًا (afflicted), Hebrew נֶאֱחֶזֶת/אֲחוּזִים (seized/held), Korean 사로잡힌 (captured by), Spanish afligidos.
